what_it_does: Many AI computations work with sparse matrices — large tables of numbers where most entries are zero and can be skipped. But the non-zero entries are scattered unpredictably, which means a chip processing them can end up with some compute units flooded with work while others sit idle. This paper, Pipirima, tries to fix that imbalance by predicting where the non-zero values will appear before they are actually read. It does this using simple hardware counters — tiny tally registers — borrowed from the same idea used in CPUs to predict which way an 'if/else' branch in a program will go. By anticipating the pattern of non-zeros while the compressed matrix data is still streaming in, the chip can schedule work more evenly across its processing units. The technique was tested on two common sparse-matrix operations: multiplying a sparse matrix by a dense vector (SpMV) and multiplying two sparse matrices (SpMM).
